title: JPM, BofA Eye Payments Deal — Why JPMorgan, Bank Of America And Other Banks Want Fiserv’s Debit Network - Stocktwits
content: Fiserv (FISV) share price gained 4% after-hours amid a report that several top financial institutions are looking to acquire a network owned by the firm to bypass federal caps on debit card transaction fees. Wall Street giants, including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and PNC Financial Services Group, have engaged in early, tentative discussions to buy a proprietary debit-card processing network from financial technology company Fiserv, according to an exclusive report by The Wall Street Journal. The move comes as banks look to replicate an edge gained by Capital One Financial following its massive $50.6-billion acquisition of Discover Financial, which granted the lender its own direct-to-merchant payment rails. At the center of the industry’s interest is a specific section of the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act known as the Durbin Amendment. The federal rule caps the interchange fees that institutions with $10 billion or more in assets can charge merchants when a consumer swipes a debit card. But under the current legal framework, if a bank owns the underlying network infrastructure, it is legally exempt from government-imposed fee limits. Consumer banks in the U.S. have fiercely fought the Durbin amendment, stating that they lose billions in revenue and are forced to eliminate popular customer perks, such as debit-card reward programs. Merchants and consumer advocacy groups have countered the claims, maintaining that lower interchange fees have directly translated to lower retail prices for the public, as per WSJ. Fiserv shares have plummeted around 70% from its 2025 highs. This decline is attributed to several factors, including a sharp deceleration in organic growth, intensifying competition in the payment point-of-sale (PoS) sector, and executive-level instability following several CEO changes. Furthermore, the company is facing significant pressure from activist investors calling for asset divestiture. However, Fiserv, is an important fintech middleman that owns two major transaction processing networks, STAR and Accel. title: Inflation, Yields and Equities: When Does the Pressure Actually Matter? - J.P. Morgan
content:

Discover our approach, digital tools and community initiatives. Equities have remained resilient despite elevated inflation and higher yields. Earnings may determine how long that resilience lasts. September’s CPI report was a reminder that the path back to 2% inflation remains uneven. Headline prices rose 0.6% on the month and 3.7% from a year earlier, with the annual measure one-tenth above consensus. Energy did much of the damage: Gasoline rose 9.1% and accounted for more than half of the monthly headline increase. The September PPI reinforced the signal: Producer prices rose 1.3% in September and 6.3% from a year earlier, with both significantly hotter than expected. In response to CPI, the market initially followed the textbook: The 2-year yield rose and the curve bear-flattened – meaning yields rose across the curve, but shorter-term yields increased more than longer-term yields. Futures roughly doubled the implied probability of an October quarter-point Federal Reserve rate hike to the mid-40% range. But the move faded through the day. By Wednesday’s close, the Treasury sell-off had reversed and October hike odds had moved back below 30%. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 was only slightly lower after CPI, then weakened as the session progressed and concerns about artificial intelligence (AI)-linked companies took over. That pressure continued despite the hot PPI print, while the Treasury curve has kept flattening – but from the other direction: Long-end yields have fallen more than front-end yields in a flight-to-safety move that began on Wednesday and extended into Thursday. The line chart shows the S&P 500 index level from 1966 to 2026 on a logarithmic y‑axis (roughly 32 to 8,192), highlighting “streaks of 60+ months above CPI 2%” and indicating the other periods. Across the first qualifying inflation regime (Feb 1966–Mar 1986, 242 months), the index trends upward; in the second qualifying regime (Feb 1987–Oct 1997, 129 months) the line rises; and in the most recent qualifying regime (Mar 2021–Sep 2026, 66 months) the index climbs. However, in all the in between periods (1986-1987 and 1997-2021), the S&P 500 increases as well. Source: JPM WM Solutions. Bloomberg Finance L.P. Data as of September 30, 2026. Past performance is no guarantee of future results. It is not possible to invest directly in an index. Across long stretches when CPI remained above 2%, the S&P 500 still compounded meaningfully. In fact, equities have historically delivered positive long-term returns even during extended periods of above-target inflation, including the current episode. It’s not that inflation is universally good for stocks, but a level of inflation above the Fed’s target says remarkably little about long-run equity returns on its own. Inflation shocks can still create sharp near-term volatility; 2022 is a clear example. Inflation still matters over time to equity performance through changes in the policy path and discount rates, as well as pressure on real household income or corporate margins. The distinction is between a rate above 2% that is relatively targeted and an inflation process that is accelerating, broadening and becoming embedded in expectations. Equities have historically been able to live with the former. The latter is where the economic and valuation damage becomes harder to contain. Similar to inflation’s effect on equities, yield levels don’t matter as much to equities as the rate of change of yield levels. Mid- to long-end Treasury yields have hit levels not seen in about two decades, and yet equities hover near all-time highs. This line chart compares cumulative S&P 500 returns over 60 trading days for 25 historical episodes resembling the current rise in the 10-year Treasury yield; the horizontal axis shows trading days from the episode start and the vertical axis shows cumulative return, with individual historical paths, their equal-weighted average, and the current rolling 30-day episode. At the latest observation, the current episode is up 1.1% versus a historical average of 0.4%; the broad spread of event lines indicates that outcomes varied considerably across comparable periods. Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P. Data as of October 14, 2026. Note: Events are the 25 closest non-overlapping historical episodes with an equal-or-larger 30-day 10-year yield rise and policy pricing within +/-1 hike-equivalent of today. Past performance is no guarantee of future results. It is not possible to invest directly in an index. Treasury sell-offs have not produced one consistent outcome for stocks. On average, the S&P 500 response has been subdued: The historical path is soft and choppy, but only basically flat 60 trading days into the move. The individual episodes, however, are highly varied – some produced meaningful drawdowns, while others were absorbed with little lasting effect. That dispersion is the point: A bond sell-off can be a headwind, but the rates move alone does not determine the equity outcome. Inflation and yields matter most for stocks when they begin to weaken demand, compress margins, raise financing costs or force analysts to cut estimates. Until those effects show up in earnings, equities can often absorb a surprising amount of macro volatility. Credit is showing some early pressure – CCC-rated bond spreads are up more than 100 basis points this year – but it remains contained. Roughly 5.5% of the high-yield index is distressed, up from 4.4% but still well below the 11% seen in 2022. The equity sell-off over the past couple of days has also been driven by AI-linked debt concerns. Essentially, credit markets are repricing policy uncertainty, while the equity market is starting to search for evidence of fundamental damage. Earnings season is therefore an important test. The first read from the large banks was broadly resilient: lending income and market-sensitive businesses provided support, while consumer credit did not show broad deterioration. The message is not that higher rates are harmless, but that the pressure remains manageable. Market concentration may also provide a near-term buffer because the largest index weights are profitable companies with significant cash generation: Only 48% of S&P 500 constituents are trading above their 200-day moving average, down from 73% just two months ago. That narrow leadership is not necessarily healthy over the long run (as we’re seeing over the past couple of days), but it can temporarily insulate the index from weakness among companies more immediately affected by higher rates and inflation. As the rest of earnings season unfolds, the key question is whether inflation is beginning to weigh on company fundamentals. Consensus still calls for S&P 500 earnings to grow roughly 30% from a year earlier, which would mark a third consecutive quarter above 25%, while estimates actually rose during the quarter rather than following their usual downward drift. Furthermore, nine of 11 sectors are expecting double-digit earnings growth this year, including the Tech sector, which is expected to grow 64%. As long as earnings hold, equities can take hotter inflation and higher yields. If guidance starts to show weaker demand, margin pressure or rising financing costs, the same inflation data will matter much more. Equities can continue to perform as long as investors continue to see tighter policy as a manageable adjustment rather than the start of a damaging cycle, and as long as earnings continue to show resilience. The first warning would be a broader inflation process: consecutive upside core readings, stronger labor-intensive services inflation or rising market- and survey-based expectations. The second would be visible credit transmission: wider high-yield spreads, deteriorating interest coverage, rising delinquencies or tighter lending standards. The third would be a break in the earnings story through negative revisions, margin compression or weaker guidance. Inflation and bond volatility are testing the equity market and will likely remain headwinds in the near term. Equities have absorbed the pressure so far, partly because of market concentration, and could continue to grind higher as long as these risks remain familiar and earnings bolster confidence. title: JPM, GS, MS Stocks Edge Higher After-Hours — Banks Lift Dividends And Announce Buybacks After Fed Stress Test - Stocktwits
content: Shares of JPMorgan Chase & Co (JPM), Morgan Stanley (MS) and Goldman Sachs (GS) edged higher in after-hours trading on Wednesday after the banks announced higher dividends and buybacks following the Federal Reserve’s stress test, which showed the banking sector remains well positioned to withstand a severe economic downturn. At the time of writing, JPM stock was up 0.6% after-hours after closing the regular session down 0.21%, while MS shares gained 0.4% and GS stock was up 0.1%. JPMorgan Chase & Co announced a $50-billion share repurchase program and raised its quarterly dividend as part of updated shareholder return plans. The bank said its board also intends to increase its quarterly dividend 10% to $1.65 per share, up from $1.50 per share, for the third quarter of 2026. The new buyback program will take effect from July 1, alongside the updated shareholder return plans. Jamie Dimon, Chairman and CEO of JPMorgan Chase, said, “The Board’s intended dividend increase is supported by our consistent investment in our business and strong financial performance. The new share repurchase program provides us with the flexibility to deploy capital in ways that enhance shareholder value over time.” Goldman Sachs (GS) also increased its quarterly dividend by 11% to $5 per share from $4.50, pointing to strong earnings momentum and a robust capital position. The revised payout implies an annual dividend of $20 and will take effect on July 1, pending board approval. Morgan Stanley (MS) similarly announced a 15% hike in its quarterly dividend to $1.15 per share from $1. In addition, the firm said its board has reauthorized a multi-year share repurchase program of up to $20 billion, with no fixed end date, set to begin in the third quarter. The announcement by JPMorgan Chase & Co comes after the U.S. Federal Reserve released the results of its annual stress test. It showed that large banks are well positioned to withstand a severe recession and continue lending to households and businesses. The Fed said that despite more than $708 billion in total loan losses under the hypothetical scenario, aggregate capital declined only 1.6 percentage points and remained above minimum requirements. It added that all 32 banks tested stayed above their minimum common equity tier 1 capital requirements under a scenario that included a severe global recession, a 39% drop in commercial real estate prices, a 30% fall in house prices and an unemployment rate peaking at 10%. Apart from the revenue targets, Qualcomm also announced a deal with Meta Platforms (META) to use its chips in AI-focused data center infrastructure. Earlier, during the regular trading session on Wednesday, QCOM shares ended 3.29% lower. The chipmaker raised its non-handset revenue target to $40 billion, about double its previous fiscal 2029 target. It also announced a comprehensive data center AI infrastructure strategy with a revenue target of more than $15 billion a year by fiscal 2029. It also set targets of over $14 billion from IoT, $8 billion from industrial, networking and robotics, and $6 billion from personal AI and compute. Qualcomm said its automotive business is on track to exit FY2026 at a $6-billion annualized revenue run rate, while its automotive design-win pipeline has grown to $65 billion. It expects automotive revenue to reach $10 billion by fiscal 2029. The company added that handsets will account for about one-third of QCT revenue by fiscal 2029, within a projected $1.7 trillion total addressable market by 2030. Qualcomm announced a deal with Meta Platforms (META) under which Qualcomm will supply data center CPUs for Meta’s infrastructure, including its Dragonfly C1000 chip. The processor is expected to power Meta’s next-generation server fleet and support future data center expansion, with production set to begin in the second half of 2028. Qualcomm said the Dragonfly C1000 is a data center CPU designed for agentic AI workloads, aimed at delivering strong computing performance while keeping power consumption low. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the company is “excited to continue partnering with Qualcomm Technologies” as it builds next-generation CPUs to support its AI ambitions. Zuckerberg added that Meta is working toward delivering “personal superintelligence to everyone in the world.” Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said the partnership reflects an expansion “from devices to data center,” calling it “just the beginning.” Qualcomm said it has secured two major hyperscaler deals that are expected to generate meaningful revenue, while its custom silicon business is projected to begin contributing meaningful revenue from Q1 2027. The company also expanded its partnership with Hugging Face to support developer-driven AI across devices and cloud infrastructure. When asked whether Coatue would keep or sell its SpaceX shares, he said, “I’m going to keep them,” noting that the shares must be held for six months after receipt. After the lockup, he said the decision becomes “more of a portfolio decision,” based on how large SpaceX becomes relative to the rest of the firm’s holdings. “We own a significant amount of SpaceX,” he said, while adding that some of his biggest mistakes came from “optimizing for the short run.” He pointed to Nvidia as a lesson, calling his decision to sell “one of the bigger mistakes” he had made. “Sometimes you’re like, ‘Oh, maybe I’m so clever. The ongoing work to renovate Chase Tower in Chicago's Loop finally has an estimated price tag of more than $800M, according to JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon. The project, alongside Google's renovation of the Thompson Center and a slew of office-to-residential conversions along LaSalle Street, is a key piece in the revitalization of downtown Chicago, which was hit hard in the aftermath of the pandemic. The bank has made big bets on its offices across the world in recent years after being at the forefront of the return-to-office charge. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. The superyacht market has no reason to be this steady. Rates have moved sharply, energy prices have swung and the macro backdrop looks meaningfully different from where it was at the start of the year. And yet, order books at the leading shipyards remain full, secondary market pricing has held and the conversations taking place around Monaco, Port Hercules continue as they always do. The question, then, is not whether the yacht market can absorb uncertainty; but rather, are buyers’ financing strategies as equally resilient? The world that owners and buyers are navigating is not the one they anticipated. Rate expectations have swung from cuts to potential hikes, and geopolitical tensions have unsettled energy markets. The first half of 2026 was defined largely by events in the Middle East, which sent energy prices spike higher. In a year of shifting narratives, attention has moved to monetary policy, where the tone has grown more hawkish than most expected. The story the market was telling in January is not the one it is telling now, and has yet to settle. This is not an environment that rewards complacency, and for superyacht owners and prospective buyers, the tension between confidence and caution is likely to shape how capital gets deployed in the months ahead. Complexity has a way of surfacing questions that calmer conditions allow people to defer. Investors will have to consider whether a financing structure has the flexibility to support broader portfolio goals — and if it can hold its shape should conditions shift again. The outlook for the superyacht market remains constructive, and this strength is structural rather than accidental. Order books at the most established shipyards extend years into the future, and that supply constraint has continued to put a floor under secondary market pricing — even as other asset classes have felt the pressure of a more volatile environment. Geopolitical uncertainty and energy price instability have not materially disrupted demand at this level of the market, and the evidence from this year suggests they are unlikely to. For buyers seeking a more immediate path to ownership, the pre-owned market offers a direct and often well-priced route. Alternatively, for those drawn to commissioning their own specifications, new builds remain available on the right timeline. However, the takeaway should be that while conditions are durable, diligent consideration should still be given to the surrounding financial mechanism of any purchase. A thoughtful approach is one that makes ownership more robust and better aligned with the broader portfolio goals that a year like this one tends to bring into focus. When rates fall, clients can capitalise on lower-cost leverage and redeploy capital toward new opportunities. When rates rise, locking in long-term fixed financing on a durable physical asset provides payment certainty and a meaningful buffer against further increases. The structure, if engineered carefully from the outset, performs across both environments rather than becoming a liability when conditions shift. For non-euro clients, currency exposure adds a further dimension that too often enters the conversation late. With the world's leading shipyards concentrated in Europe, recent dollar movements have made hedging a necessary component of any comprehensive financing structure, not a refinement to be addressed once contracts are signed. More broadly, the logic of yacht financing rests on preserving liquidity and maintaining optionality: avoiding the concentration of capital in a single asset and keeping flexibility intact across a broader portfolio. Some clients want a partner to navigate the complexity of a major build alongside them, whereas others are focused on keeping their broader investment architecture intact. A structure designed carefully from the outset serves both, and throughout periods of uncertainty as we have recently seen, that adaptability is paramount. Uncertainty is a reason to structure well, not to wait. Our conversations with clients begin with a single question: What should your wealth accomplish, and how does yacht financing fit within that picture? When that question is answered clearly, the asset supports the plan rather than complicating it. After all, the seas are often rough. The point is to be built to weather the storm. In uncertain markets, specialty lending prices risk by focusing on durability and flexibility: the underlying asset’s resilience (e.g., a durable physical asset), payment certainty through long-term fixed financing when appropriate, and structures that can “hold their shape” if rates or narratives shift again. Lenders navigate changing markets by anticipating shifting narratives (rates, geopolitics, energy) and building adaptable specialty lending structures early — addressing interest-rate strategy up front and, for non-euro clients, integrating currency hedging as a core component rather than a late-stage add-on. The protections that matter most are those that preserve resilience and clarity under volatility: payment certainty (often via long-term fixed-rate structures), disciplined up-front structuring to avoid surprises later, and safeguards that keep broader portfolio flexibility intact rather than concentrating capital in a single asset. Superyacht financing adds market- and execution-specific risks: long timelines for new builds, reliance on shipyard schedules, and — especially for non-euro clients — meaningful currency exposure because leading shipyards are concentrated in Europe, making hedging a necessary part of a comprehensive structure. The superyacht market has held its course for structural reasons: leading shipyards’ order books extend years out, constraining supply and putting a floor under secondary market pricing, while this year’s geopolitical and energy volatility has not materially disrupted demand at the top end. Master trust filings are the monthly window into securitised credit card performance, and a sequential decline in net charge-offs of this size sits within the normal range of month-to-month variation rather than marking a trend break on its own. Historically the card charge-off series has been one of the cleaner real-time reads on the consumer, with deterioration tending to show first in delinquencies before feeding through to charge-offs with a lag of a few months, so the delinquency line in the same filing is the more forward-looking tell. A single month's improvement after a stretch of rising loss rates has, in past cycles, often proved to be noise rather than inflection; the pattern that matters is several consecutive prints moving together across issuers, since idiosyncratic portfolio mix and seasonal factors can move one trust independently of the cohort. For the large card issuers this series is read against the pace of reserve builds and the guidance embedded in card revenue, rather than against the quarter's headline numbers. The follow-ons are the comparable monthly trust filings from the peer card issuers and the next round of delinquency data, which together separate issuer-specific movement from a genuine turn in consumer credit.

The firm assigned JPMorgan a “Wide” Economic Moat rating, pointing to the reputation of its investment banking franchise, cost advantages in consumer and commercial banking, and significant switching costs across its operations. Morningstar also sees multiple growth drivers ahead, including branch expansion, stronger deposit gathering, growing customer product penetration, and continued growth in fee-based businesses. Veteran investor George Noble believes Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's first policy meeting marked a major shift in the central bank’s approach and “nobody is paying attention.” In a Substack post, the former associate of Fidelity’s Peter Lynch said Warsh’s refusal to provide a dot plot, a chart that shows where the central bank’s top policymakers think the short-term interest rates are headed, is a deviation from the Fed’s long-term approach. “For 15 years, investors have been spoonfed forward guidance by a Fed that practically held their hand through every meeting. That era ended in a single afternoon,” Noble said. In its latest policy meeting, the Federal Reserve left key interest rates unchanged at 3.50% - 3.75%, with the latest projections indicating one rate increase in 2026, although Warsh did not provide his projections to the dot plot. According to Noble, this was significant. “Without lifting a finger on the short term rate, Warsh sent 10 year TIPS yields spiking the moment he stopped talking,” Noble said. “This is the higher for longer regime made explicit.” Noble argued that Warsh has shown the Fed can tighten financial conditions without raising interest rates, simply by reducing guidance, and allowing markets to reprice risk on their own. He also said that he expects inflation to remain elevated while economic growth broadens through manufacturing and reshoring, with the Fed relying more on communication than rate hikes to curb speculation. “None of this is bearish for the market but it is absolutely bearish for the parts of the market that have feasted on cheap money and forward guidance for the last fifteen years,” he said. The investor also warned that the change in the regime’s stance would make investors concentrated in long-duration technology stocks and passive index funds vulnerable. “If your portfolio is still built around long duration tech and passive index exposure, you are positioned for a regime that ended on Wednesday afternoon,” he said. Instead of investing in the AI-heavy S&P 500, Noble said that businesses with strong free cash flow, pricing power, durable competitive advantages, and tangible assets are better positioned for a market environment shaped by higher real yields and less Fed support. “You want businesses that throw off real cash flow without needing to spend their entire operating budget on the next round of GPUs. You want tangible assets that cannot be disrupted by an AI startup with a clever prompt. You want pricing power, limited competition, and long duration cash flows that compound regardless of what the front end of the curve does,” he added. Red Cat Holdings (RCAT) stock is headed toward its weakest month this year, with shares dropping about 23% during June as investors weigh the effects of tightening global supply chains against strong demand for defense technology. The decline comes even as the drone maker expands production, launches new drone systems, and secures additional international business. Market concerns have intensified after China's Ministry of Commerce said on Monday that it is banning exports of dual-use products to 10 U.S. defense and technology firms, including Red Cat Holdings and its Teal Drones unit. The move comes in response to Washington's decision to place additional Chinese firms on a Pentagon list of businesses allegedly linked to China's military. The curb means Chinese-made dual-use goods can no longer be supplied to these companies by any seller worldwide, and any existing export shipments or transactions must stop immediately. Although Red Cat's drones meet U.S. defense standards and do not rely on Chinese technology, investors remain concerned about supply chain issues. As more Western companies look for non-Chinese sources of specialized parts and materials, competition for those limited supplies has become more intense. Red Cat stock traded over 1% lower overnight, heading into Monday. Despite the stock's decline this month, Red Cat continues to expand its operations. The company last week introduced its new Hellcat unmanned aircraft system at the Eurosatory defense exhibition in Paris, positioning the platform for operations in heavily contested electronic warfare environments. The Hellcat system builds on Red Cat's existing Black Widow platform and is designed for military and government customers operating in environments where GPS signals may be unavailable or disrupted. Shares of Butterfly Network (BFLY) logged their best day ever on Thursday after the company revealed that its technology is powering Midjourney's ambitious new healthcare venture, a full-body imaging platform that has already drawn praise from famed investor Michael Burry. BFLY stock surged 56% on Thursday, with shares coming off their strongest week ever and remaining on track for their best year to date. BFLY was also up more than 2% in overnight trading heading into Monday. "I am a fan of Midjourney, but wow. Read until the end," Burry said on X, referring to the company’s latest healthcare announcement. "This is indeed how medicine and health care can be reimagined in this new paradigm of untold processing power." Midjourney, best known for its AI image-generation platform, unveiled Midjourney Medical and a new whole-body scanner that makes advanced health imaging faster, cheaper and more accessible. Butterfly said the current Midjourney Scanner prototype uses 40 of its proprietary Ultrasound-on-Chip imaging modules under a co-development agreement. The company noted that future versions are expected to incorporate substantially more imaging modules as the platform scales. Importantly, Butterfly previously said that the partnership could generate up to $74 million in payments over five years. "We're proud to support Midjourney's mission to democratize access to personal imaging data," CEO Joseph DeVivo said, adding that the roadmap unveiled by Midjourney represents a "potentially meaningful commercial opportunity" for Butterfly. Midjourney's scanner aims to deliver detailed whole-body images using ultrasound rather than radiation or magnetic fields. The company says users would step into a pool of warm water and pass through a ring containing roughly 500,000 ultrasonic sensors, generating terabytes of imaging data that are processed using AI and high-performance computing. The goal is a scan lasting about 60 seconds, producing MRI-like body maps at a fraction of the cost and with far greater accessibility. Midjourney also plans to deploy the tech through dedicated wellness centers called Midjourney Spas. The first location is expected to open in San Francisco in 2027, combining traditional spa amenities with routine body scanning. "We've dreamed of something as powerful as MRI, and as casual as a trip to the spa," Midjourney founder David Holz said. The company plans to launch a research spa in 2027, expand to additional cities in 2028 and ultimately deploy more advanced scanner generations built on custom silicon. By 2031, Midjourney is looking to operate over 50,000 scanners worldwide with the capacity to perform up to one billion scans per month. For comparison, 100 million to 150 million MRI scans are performed worldwide each year, according to Par Kragsterman, CTO at Collective Minds Radiology, a medical imaging research platform. If achieved, Midjourney's target capacity would be 80x to 120x larger than today's global MRI market.
